fullName: Coherent High-Energy X-ray Sector for In Situ Science

status2026.detail: All four branches received first light in July 2025 (r12). On the APS Beamline Commissioning Progress chart of 5 Oct 2026, 28-ID-B,C and 28-ID-F are at stage 5 ('Scientific Commissioning and Early Experiments') and 28-ID-D,E and 28-ID-G at stage 4 ('Technical Commissioning'); none is yet in stage 6 (general user program) (r11). In Jan 2026 all four were at stage 4 (r25). The Beamline Directory still lists B/C as 'Not Currently Operational' and D/E, F, G as 'Under Development', on-site access (r6-r9). CHEX was delivered within the APS-U project scope (project formally completed Jan 2026; r25, r14). The sector currently runs on interim permanent-magnet undulators (2.8 cm upstream, 3.0 cm downstream; ID table updated 22 Sep 2026, r10); the baseline 18.5 mm superconducting undulator pair was delayed by SCU core-reliability issues and is planned for 2026-2027 (r13). The 2025-2 proposal call (Jan 2025) already offered a 'Feature Beamlines' proposal type for CHEX (r23). Timeline note: the Aug 2025 update projected first experiments late 2025/early 2026 and entry into the general user program late in run 2026-1 or early in run 2026-2 (r12); as of the 5 Oct 2026 chart no CHEX station has reached stage 6, so that projection has slipped.

tagline: Laser-like, high-energy X-rays that watch new materials being built atom by atom inside working reactors.
plainSummary: CHEX is a family of X-ray stations built to watch materials being made and changed in real time: crystal films growing in a hot gas reactor, oxide layers stacking up in a vacuum chamber, a battery electrode charging. It combines two things the upgraded APS does better than any other X-ray source. First, high energy: CHEX's X-rays (mostly 15 to 105 thousand electron-volts) go straight through quartz reactor walls, gases and liquids, so experiments can run inside real growth machines instead of in an idealised vacuum. Second, coherence: the new APS electron beam is so small that its X-rays march in step, a bit like laser light. When such a beam bounces off a material it makes a grainy 'speckle' pattern that is a fingerprint of exactly where atoms, islands and defects sit, and as the speckles flicker you can see them move. Two undulators feed four branch beamlines and eight experiment spots, so up to four teams can work at once and slow, complicated growth experiments can stay set up for days.
expertSummary: CHEX (28-ID) is a canted-undulator sector (1 mrad) optimized for coherent scattering at 15-105 keV, multiplexed into four simultaneously operating branches and eight instrument positions for in situ synthesis and processing studies. The upstream (outboard) source feeds the tunable branch 28-ID-A/B/C through a horizontally deflecting, LN2-cooled fixed-exit DCM (Si(111)/(311)) at 35 m; the downstream (inboard) source feeds three fixed-energy branches through thin single-crystal side-bounce monochromators at 28.3 m (diamond, D/E), 38.3 m (diamond, F) and 40.2 m (Si, G) that transmit unused flux downstream. Nearly fixed scattering angles (2θ ≈ 22.7-23.2° for diamond, ≈4.9-5.0° for Si) let a change of reflection (111/220/400) select odd harmonics of a common ~5 keV fundamental (the reflection ratios √3:√8:√16 match the harmonic ratios 3:5:7 to within ~2%, so a small re-angling is still needed): 15 keV (D/E), 25/35 keV (F), 75/105 keV (G). Every position has a two-element CRL 'zoom' (CRL1 just downstream of each SCM inside 28-ID-A, or at 50 m in the mini-enclosure SE-1 for B/C; CRL2 1.5-2.5 m before the sample; Ni lenses on G in the FDR design) giving ~1-15 µm (H) × 0.3-5 µm (V) foci at fixed focal plane, sized so speckle is resolved by ~55 µm pixels at 1-4 m. Shared instruments are Huber hexapod diffractometers with a long-distance detector positioner; integrated chambers include oxide MBE (C), PLD + HAXPES (E) and MOCVD (F); tandem hutches with moveable stops allow access to rear stations while front stations run. As of Oct 2026 the sector runs on interim 2.8/3.0 cm HPMUs pending the 18.5 mm SCU pair; B/C and F are in scientific commissioning.

whatAPSUEnables.plain: On the old APS only about one high-energy X-ray in ten thousand was 'in step' (coherent). To see speckle from a growing gallium-nitride crystal at 25 keV, scientists had to remove the monochromator and accept a 'pink' beam (the undulator's whole third-harmonic peak, about 1% spread in energy, instead of one sharp colour), and still needed 10-second exposures. The upgrade made the electron beam about 20 times narrower and four times better collimated in its wide direction (a ~70-fold drop in 'emittance'), so the coherent part of the beam at 20-25 keV is now a few hundred times stronger. That turns speckle movies at energies that can see inside real reactors from a heroic stunt into a routine measurement - and fast enough to follow atoms while a film grows. CHEX is the APS-U beamline designed specifically to cash in that gain at high energy.
whatAPSUEnables.expert: Coherent flux scales as F_coh ≈ B·(λ/2)², so the 15-60+ keV regime needed to penetrate quartz, steel and liquid cells was coherence-starved on the 3 nm·rad ring. APS-U (εeff 42 pm vs 3113 pm) raises coherent flux at 20 keV by ~540× (FDR Table 1.1). The pre-upgrade benchmark (Ju et al. 2019, 12-ID-D) needed pink beam (ΔE/E = 1.3×10^-2) to reach 1.4×10^12 ph/s at 25.75 keV with 1.2 × 2.7 µm coherence lengths and 10 s frames. Because XPCS SNR ∝ β·I_pix·sqrt(Δt·N_pix·T) (r29, r27), a ~10² gain in coherent intensity can buy up to ~10⁴ shorter delay times at constant SNR, or monochromatic operation with full speckle contrast. The small source (σx ≈ 12-15 µm rms; nearly round only in round-beam mode, 12.3 × 8.3 µm, vs 14.5 × 3.1 µm in flat-beam mode, r15) plus dual-CRL optics delivers speckle-resolving foci (a ≤ 0.886λR/p ≈ 20·R[m]/E[keV] µm for 55 µm pixels; PDR) at R = 2-4 m. Harmonic multiplexing with transmissive diamond SCMs converts the brightness gain into beam time: four long-duration in situ experiments run simultaneously from one straight section.
quantitative: Coherent flux at 20 keV: 312 × 10^11 ph/s (APS-U brightness mode) vs 0.6 × 10^11 ph/s (pre-upgrade APS), a factor ≈540 (r3, FDR Table 1.1)

Effective emittance 42 pm (APS-U design, brightness mode) vs 3113 pm pre-upgrade (r3); measured 45 pm·rad at 50 mA and as low as 28 pm·rad in round-beam mode, vs 134 pm·rad previous record at ESRF-EBS (r16). Note: the 28 pm·rad round-beam figure is the per-plane value (εx = εy = 28.7 pm, r15) - the emittance is shared equally between the two planes, it is not a lower total

Calculated coherent fraction at 25 keV ≈ 2% (APS-U flat beam, 2.07 m HPMU) vs ≈ 0.01% (old APS, 2.4 m undulator) - ~200×; at 60 keV ≈ 0.6% vs ≈ 0.002% - ~300× (our Gaussian-beam estimate from r15 and r3 source parameters, zero energy spread; indicative only)
Pre-upgrade benchmark: GaN growth XPCS at 25.75 keV required pink beam (ΔE/E = 1.3%), 1.4 × 10^12 ph/s in a 4 × 16 µm spot, 10 s frames (r17)
Ju et al. 2017: with APS-U the coherent flux at 12-ID-D-type energies would approach the total flux then available; the optimum energy for coherent flux through 4 mm of fused quartz is ≈23 keV (r18)
FDR design (SCU source) at 28-ID-B: 6.8-37 × 10^12 ph/s at 15 keV and 4.2-11 × 10^12 ph/s at 60 keV into 0.8-9.8 µm (H) × 0.3-3.4 µm (V) FWHM foci (r1, Table 4.10)
Four simultaneously operating experiments from one sector (eight positions), vs a single goniometer/instrument on comparable coherent beamlines such as ESRF ID01 (PDR comparison, r4; r5)

Scaling estimate: since XPCS SNR grows linearly with coherent intensity per pixel and only as the square root of frame time, a 100× coherent-intensity gain can shorten the shortest measurable correlation time by up to ~10^4 at constant SNR (r27 scaling; indicative)

techniques.name: X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (surface / grazing-incidence)
techniques.plain: Shine a laser-like X-ray beam on a surface and film the flickering speckle pattern. How fast the speckles change tells you how fast atoms, islands or domains are moving - even when, on average, nothing seems to change.
techniques.expert: Intensity autocorrelation g2(q,τ) = <I(t)I(t+τ)>/<I>² = 1 + β|f(q,τ)|² for stationary dynamics; for non-equilibrium growth CHEX relies on two-time correlations C(q,t1,t2). Surface XPCS near CTR anti-Bragg positions probes island/step dynamics during MOVPE, PLD, MBE, sputtering or etching. Contrast β is set by coherence lengths vs illuminated volume, bandwidth and pixel size; SNR ∝ β I_pix sqrt(Δt N_pix T) (Lumma et al. 2000, r29; reviewed in r27).

techniques.name: Coherent diffraction imaging, Bragg CDI and Bragg ptychography
techniques.plain: Record the speckle pattern around a single tiny crystal and let a computer turn it back into a 3-D picture of the crystal - including maps of how its atoms are squeezed or stretched.
techniques.expert: Oversampled (≥2×) coherent diffraction about a Bragg peak is phased iteratively to recover the complex density ρ(r)e^{iQ·u(r)}, giving 3-D displacement/strain fields of nanocrystals or grains in operando; high energy enables penetration of cells and access to multiple reflections. Requires speckle-resolving geometry: the coherently illuminated region (the beam spot, or the isolated crystal if it is smaller) must be ≤ 0.886λR/p ≈ 20·R[m]/E[keV] µm for 55 µm pixels (PDR), and about half that for the ≥2× oversampling CDI needs; plus sub-µm sample stability.

techniques.name: In situ surface X-ray diffraction / crystal-truncation-rod scattering
techniques.plain: X-rays bouncing off a crystal surface carry a signature of the top few atomic layers. During layer-by-layer growth that signal pulses once per completed atomic layer - an atomic-scale stopwatch.
techniques.expert: Specular and non-specular CTR and diffuse scattering at 15-35 keV through chamber walls; anti-Bragg intensity oscillates with monolayer period during layer-by-layer growth (ideal kinematic case I ∝ |1-2θcov|²). Tunable branch adds resonant/anomalous contrast for multi-cation oxides (PDR).

techniques.name: High-energy X-ray diffraction
techniques.plain: Very-high-energy X-rays (75-105 keV) go through centimetres of material, so you can study crystals deep inside furnaces, reactors or thick samples.
techniques.expert: 28-ID-G at 75/105 keV (Si 022/004) for bulk synthesis, crystal growth, corrosion and mechanical/environmental loading; small Bragg angles, large Q-range on area detectors; Ni CRL focusing.

techniques.name: X-ray reflection interface microscopy
techniques.plain: A zone-plate 'X-ray microscope objective' behind the sample makes a real-space image of an interface using X-rays reflected from it - showing steps and domains at a buried surface.
techniques.expert: Full-field imaging of interfaces using specular/CTR reflectivity contrast; FDR XRIM configuration places a zone-plate objective on the diffractometer detector arm and the PAD on the LDDP; proposed with BCDI for geochemical interfaces (PDR Table 6.9).

techniques.name: Hard X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (with PLD)
techniques.plain: X-rays knock electrons out of the growing film; measuring their energies tells you the chemistry and electronic state of atoms buried under the surface.
techniques.expert: At 28-ID-E a 'twisted monochromator' provides 10 keV for HAXPES alongside in situ PLD/SXRD (Directory); the published system used 4-12 keV and a Scienta EW4000 analyser to correlate electronic structure with structure during oxide heterostructure growth (Eres et al. 2019).

scienceCases.title: Crystals with a memory: island patterns during layer-by-layer growth
scienceCases.plain: When gallium nitride grows one atomic layer at a time, tiny islands appear on each new layer. Coherent X-ray 'speckle movies' showed that each layer's islands tend to form where the previous layer's islands were - the crystal remembers.
scienceCases.expert: Ju et al. (Nature Phys. 2019) measured two-time correlations of diffuse speckle near the (H 0 -H 0) specular rod at H = 0.48 (just off anti-Bragg) during homoepitaxial MOVPE of m-plane GaN (25.75 keV, pink beam, 10 s frames) and found oscillating correlations that reveal persistent island arrangements between successive monolayers, explained by adatom-mediated interlayer communication (Ehrlich-Schwoebel barrier). CHEX's MOCVD station in 28-ID-F is designed to extend this with far higher coherent flux.

scienceCases.title: Oxide films that rearrange their own layers
scienceCases.plain: Researchers trying to stack oxide layers in a chosen order found, by watching with X-rays during growth, that the layers swap places on their own - and used that trick to make a crystal never grown before.
scienceCases.expert: Lee et al. (Nature Mater. 2014) used in situ X-ray scattering during oxide MBE at APS 33-ID-E to show dynamic layer rearrangement in Ruddlesden-Popper growth and synthesised single-crystal La3Ni2O7 films. The oxide-MBE program (H. Hong) now has a station at 28-ID-C on the tunable branch, where resonant contrast helps distinguish cations.

scienceCases.title: Following electrons and oxygen vacancies while oxide heterostructures grow
scienceCases.plain: A laser builds oxide films puff by puff while X-rays measure both where the atoms go and what the electrons are doing - key for 'dead layers' that spoil thin-film electronics.
scienceCases.expert: Eres et al. (RSI 2019) combined PLD, real-time SXRD and in situ HAXPES (4-12 keV) and demonstrated oxygen-vacancy-driven perovskite↔brownmillerite transformations in La2/3Sr1/3MnO3 capped with SrTiO3-δ. 28-ID-E hosts a PLD diffractometer with HAXPES fed by a 10 keV 'twisted' monochromator.

scienceCases.title: Growing better qubit crystals
scienceCases.plain: Silicon carbide can host quantum bits, but it is hard to grow perfectly. CHEX lets scientists look inside the growth environment as the crystal forms.
scienceCases.expert: The APS CHEX page highlights in situ studies of SiC growth for qubit hosts; 2021 CHEX workshops covered MOCVD/ALD/catalysts/SiC.

scienceCases.title: Chips: watching deposition and etching
scienceCases.plain: Computer chips are made by depositing and etching films a few atoms thick. CHEX can watch those steps happen, showing where defects and strain are born.
scienceCases.expert: APS Strategic Plan 2025-29: in situ surface scattering and XPCS of deposition and etching at CHEX to probe crystallization, defect formation and strain evolution during microelectronics fabrication steps.

scienceCases.title: Batteries, fuel cells and electrochemistry under operating conditions
scienceCases.plain: Coherent X-rays can image a single battery particle in 3-D while it charges, revealing defects that move and strain that builds up. CHEX brings this to higher energies that see through real cells.
scienceCases.expert: Ulvestad et al. (Science 2015) used BCDI to follow dislocation dynamics in operando LiNi0.5Mn1.5O4 nanoparticles; the PDR cites this as a model for CHEX, where 15-35 keV beams (the energy need listed for electrochemistry and catalysis in PDR Table 6.9) penetrate electrolyte and cell hardware for solid-solid, liquid-solid and vapor-solid interface studies (Fister, Markovic, Zhou community).

scienceCases.title: Rocks, corrosion and materials in harsh environments
scienceCases.plain: From carbon storage in rocks to rusting steel, many important reactions happen in messy, hidden places. High-energy coherent X-rays can image them at the nanoscale as they happen.
scienceCases.expert: PDR science case: coherent imaging of mineral-fluid reactivity in porous geomaterials, corrosion (costs >3% of US GDP) and nuclear materials under load using 35-60 keV beams; an environmental load frame and combined XRIM/BCDI instrument were proposed (Table 6.9).

source.canting: Two IDs canted by 1 mrad (0.5 mrad end magnets, 1 mrad centre magnet); upstream ID → outboard beam (tunable branch), downstream ID → inboard beam (fixed-energy branches).
source.frontEnd: APS-U canted-undulator front end (CUFE), windowless with differential pumping; limits 2 × 10 kW and 280 kW/mrad²; GRID XBPM1 + XBPM2 in exit mask; exit mask 2 × 1 mm (H × V) per beam (CHEX requirement; standard 2 × 2 mm), apertures 1 mrad apart, at 25.4-25.6 m; tungsten exit collimator 5 × 5 mm at 26.0 m. An APS-U-design CUFE was installed at 28-ID and tested with beam on the pre-upgrade ring in Nov 2018 (FDR milestone MS-L2-2300, r3; r2 Sec. 3-2.2.1).
source.sourceSizeAndDivergence: Electron beam at an ID straight (r15, Aug 2024): round-beam mode σx = 12.3 µm, σy = 8.26 µm, σx' = 2.34 µrad, σy' = 3.47 µrad (ε = 28.7 pm each plane); flat-beam mode (κ = 0.1) σx = 14.5 µm, σy = 3.08 µm, σx' = 2.75 µrad, σy' = 1.29 µrad. FDR Table 1.1 brightness mode: 14.7 µm / 3.2 µm / 2.8 µrad / 1.3 µrad. Single-electron photon contribution for a 2.07 m undulator at 25 keV ≈ 1.1 µm and 3.5 µrad (calculated, σr = sqrt(2λL)/4π, σr' = sqrt(λ/2L)). Canted sources sit ~1.23 m either side of the straight centre; PDR optics designs assumed 50 µm FWHM horizontal source.

branches.name: 28-ID-A/B/C - tunable-energy branch
branches.description: Outboard canted beam (upstream undulator) → horizontal LN2-cooled DCM at 35 m → straight ahead through a shielded white-beam transport (43.5-60.6 m, through hutch G) with its own mini-enclosure for transfocator 1 (50 m) → tandem hutches 28-ID-B (shared hexapod diffractometer, 64.5 m) and 28-ID-C (oxide MBE, 72 m). White/pink-beam rated (moveable WB stop at 69.3 m). Energy 5-60 keV (FDR), currently 6-30 keV listed.

branches.name: Inboard canted beam (shared)
branches.description: Beam of the downstream undulator, 1 mrad inboard of the tunable beam, filtered by 2 mm graphite. It runs through 28-ID-A and is tapped successively by three transmissive single-crystal monochromators (28.3, 38.3, 40.2 m), each set to a different harmonic of the same undulator fundamental.

branches.name: 28-ID-A/D/E - fixed 15 keV
branches.description: Diamond (111) SCM at 28.3 m deflects ~23.2° outboard; CRL1 in A; tandem hutches 28-ID-D (Huber hexapod diffractometer, 35.5 m) and 28-ID-E (PLD + HAXPES, 43.0 m); a 10 keV 'twisted' monochromator serves HAXPES.

branches.description: Diamond (022)/(004) SCM at 38.3 m deflects ~23° outboard; one hutch 28-ID-F with two positions F/1 (45.5 m, Huber hexapod diffractometer) and F/2 (49.5 m), hosting the MOCVD growth chamber.

components.name: Upstream undulator (as-built interim): 2.8 cm hybrid permanent-magnet undulator 'APS28#11S'
components.distanceNote: approx: canted-pair ID centres sit ~1.23 m either side of the straight-section centre (FDR Fig. 3.11: -1229.5/+1234.5 mm for 2.1 m canted HPMUs); FDR Table 4.4 gives ±1.25 m for the planned SCUs
components.plain: A 2-metre row of alternating magnets that wiggles the 6 GeV electrons so they emit an intense, narrow X-ray beam. This one feeds the tunable-energy branch.
components.expert: Short canted hybrid permanent-magnet undulator, 28 mm period, 74 periods (~2.07 m), device min gap 8.5 mm (user min 9.0 mm); Keff 2.49 and E1 = 2.98 keV at min gap; 9.0 kW total, 201 kW/mrad² on axis at 200 mA. Interim device: the FDR baseline is an 18.5 mm-period, 1.3 m NbTi superconducting undulator (SCU) in a shared canted cryostat. Upstream ID of a canted pair → outboard beam (APS convention, FDR 6-ID/34-ID text) → 28-ID-A/B/C; corroborated by FDR Table 4.13 (HDCM absorbs 697 W ≈ upstream SCU's 698 W).

components.name: Canting magnets (0.5 mrad + 1 mrad + 0.5 mrad)
components.distanceNote: approx: end magnets at each end of the ~5.4 m straight, 1 mrad magnet at its centre (FDR 3-3.3.5)
components.plain: Small steering magnets that nudge the electron beam so the two undulators shine in slightly different directions - just 1 milliradian apart - giving two independent X-ray beams.
components.expert: Standard APS-U canted geometry: 0.5 mrad canting magnets at the upstream and downstream ends and a 1 mrad canting magnet (with corrector) between the two IDs; beams separate by 1 mrad × z (≈28 mm at 28 m, ≈65 mm at 64.5 m). For the SCU baseline the centre canting magnet sits inside the shared 4.8 m cryostat at cryogenic temperature.

components.name: Downstream undulator (as-built interim): 3.0 cm hybrid permanent-magnet undulator 'APS30#6S'
components.distanceNote: approx: see us-undulator
components.plain: The second magnet array. Its beam is shared by three fixed-energy branches: each crystal along the way skims off one X-ray colour and lets the rest pass.
components.expert: Short canted hybrid PMU, 30 mm period, 69 periods (~2.07 m), device min gap 9.0 mm (admin min 9.0, user min 12.0 mm in the Sep-2026 table); Keff 2.64, E1 = 2.54 keV at min gap; 9.0 kW, 188 kW/mrad². For harmonic multiplexing the fundamental is set near 5 keV (K≈1.6) so the 3rd/5th/7th harmonics hit 15/25/35 keV and the 15th/21st hit 75/105 keV. Planned replacement: SCU 18.5 mm × 1.3 m with Ky = 2.291 (E1 = 5.1 keV, FDR Table 4.13).

geometryNotes: Plan view (FDR Fig. 4.2, confirmed by the 2025 as-built ray-trace r14): the straight-ahead axis carries the OUTBOARD canted beam (upstream ID) through 28-ID-A (≈23.6-43.4 m), a shielded transport running along the outboard side of hutch G (43.5-60.6 m, with the mini-enclosure SE-1 at 48.2-52.2 m) and on into tandem hutches B (≈60.7-69.5 m) and C (≈69.7-78.6 m). The INBOARD beam (downstream ID) runs 1 mrad inboard of it (lateral separation ≈ 1 mrad × z: ~28 mm at 28 m, ~40 mm at 40 m) and is tapped by three side-bounce SCMs inside A: D/E at 28.3 m and F at 38.3 m deflect it ~23.2° OUTBOARD (away from the ring, toward the experiment-hall outer wall and the control rooms), so these two branches cross over the tunable beam within centimetres of their crystals and leave A through its outboard wall (approx. D/E at ~33.4 m path, F at ~42.5 m path, scaled from FDR Fig. 4.2); G at 40.2 m deflects ~5° INBOARD (toward the ring) into the long G hutch alongside the tunable transport. All tabulated distances are path lengths along each branch from the straight-section centre (sources actually at ≈±1.23 m). Model branch start points: D/E (28.3 m, +23.2°), F (38.3 m, +23.0°), G (40.2 m, -5.0°), positive = outboard. Hutches D and E (and F) are rotated ~23° relative to the main axis; D/E is a tandem pair, F and G are single long hutches with two instrument positions each (front instruments retract in 'beam-pass' mode). Each station has a control room; D, E, F control rooms and a Sample Prep Lab lie outboard; B outboard, C and G inboard. CHEX spreads over floor normally used by 28-BM/29-BM (no BM lines there) and the short neighbouring 27-ID (r4). Every station has a CRL2 + slit + window 1.5-2.5 m upstream of its sample (beamline vacuum ends at the window). The tunable DCM is horizontal fixed-exit, so the tunable mono beam is laterally displaced (a 2025 ray-trace note mentions shifting a photon mask 4-8 mm outboard for monochromatic mode - low-resolution reading). Beam height ≈1.4 m. Naming caution: the 2017 PDR used different station letters (fixed branches B/C, D, E; tunable F/G) - this dossier uses the FDR/as-built names. Pre-upgrade, 28-ID was unoccupied (2017) and hosted the IDEA optics-test beamline until the 2023 shutdown; the CUFE and FOE 28-ID-A were built early (2018-2019).

interactiveIdeas.title: One rainbow, four experiments: the harmonic multiplexer
interactiveIdeas.concept: A slider sets the undulator gap (fundamental E1, 2-8 keV) and shows the comb of harmonics n·E1. Three crystals sit in the beam at fixed angles (diamond at 2θ = 23.2°, silicon at 2θ = 5.0°); the visitor clicks a crystal to swap reflections (111/220/400). Each branch lights up only when a harmonic lands on its Bragg energy; at E1 ≈ 5 keV all three branches glow at once (15, 25/35, 75/105 keV) while the unused light passes through the diamonds to the next crystal.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why CHEX can run several fixed-energy experiments off one undulator, and how a crystal acts like a colour filter.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: E[keV] = 12.398/λ[Å]; Bragg λ = 2d sinθ with d = a/sqrt(h²+k²+l²), a(C) = 3.5668 Å, a(Si) = 5.4310 Å; harmonics E_n = n·E1 with E1[keV] = 0.9496·E_e²[GeV]/(λu[cm](1+K²/2)); C(111)@15 keV → 2θ = 23.15°, C(220)@25 keV → 22.68°, C(400)@35 keV → 22.91°, Si(220)@75 keV → 4.93°, Si(400)@105 keV → 4.98° (PDR Tables 6.10/6.13): (111)/(220)/(400) match harmonic ratios 3:5:7 only approximately, so show the ±0.5° mismatch; Si/diamond forbidden reflections (e.g. 200) carry no intensity; even harmonics weak on-axis; finite energy spread broadens high harmonics (n = 15-21).

interactiveIdeas.title: Speckle needs a tiny spot
interactiveIdeas.concept: Visitor adjusts X-ray energy, focal-spot size (via a zoom-lens knob) and detector distance; a simulated speckle pattern is rendered on a 55 µm pixel grid. When the spot is too big the speckles shrink below a pixel and wash out; the meter shows contrast β collapsing.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why CHEX needs micron focusing, long hutches and small pixels - and why higher energy makes coherent imaging harder.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Speckle angular size ≈ λ/a; resolve when λR/a ≳ p: a_max = 0.886λR/p ≈ 20·R[m]/E[keV] µm for p = 55 µm (PDR); e.g. 35 keV, R = 4 m → a ≤ 2.3 µm; oversampling ≥2 for CDI; coherence length ξ ≈ λz/(2πσ) (Gaussian Schell; other conventions differ by π); coherent flux ∝ B·λ² ∝ E^-2 at fixed brightness.

interactiveIdeas.title: Grow a crystal, watch the clock
interactiveIdeas.concept: A 3-D surface where atoms rain down and islands nucleate, grow and coalesce layer by layer. Linked plots show the anti-Bragg CTR intensity oscillating once per monolayer, the diffuse-speckle pattern, and a two-time correlation map building up in real time; a toggle compares 'no memory' vs 'memory' island nucleation (Ju et al. 2019).
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How X-rays count atomic layers and how coherent speckle reveals hidden correlations between successive layers.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Kinematic anti-Bragg amplitude for layer-by-layer growth: I ∝ |1 - 2θ|² for fractional coverage θ of the top layer (period = 1 ML); diffuse island scattering oscillates out of phase with the CTR, peaking at half-integer ML; two-time correlation as defined by Ju et al. 2019: C(t1,t2) = <ΔI(Q,t1)ΔI(Q,t2)> / <Ī(Q,t1)Ī(Q,t2)>, with ΔI = I - Ī and Ī the pixel-smoothed mean, so the diagonal equals the speckle contrast; C > 0, = 0, < 0 means correlated, uncorrelated, anti-correlated island arrangements, and persistent arrangements give a 'checkerboard' of off-diagonal correlations with a 1 ML period; GaN growth rate in the benchmark was ~1.25×10^-3 ML/s, frames 10 s (r17).

interactiveIdeas.title: The X-ray zoom lens
interactiveIdeas.concept: Two transfocator stacks (CRL1 far upstream, CRL2 1.5 m before the sample). The visitor flips lenses in and out of each stack; the focal spot on the sample zooms from ~10 µm to <1 µm while staying in the same plane. A second mode shows how lenses focus each harmonic at a different distance so a slit near the focus rejects unwanted harmonics.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: How refractive lenses focus X-rays, why many lenses are needed at high energy, and why G uses nickel instead of beryllium.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Thin-lens focal length f = R/(2Nδ) for N biconcave paraboloids of apex radius R; δ ≈ r_e λ² n_e/2π (Be: δ ≈ 1.5×10^-6 at 15 keV, ≈ 2.8×10^-7 at 35 keV; δ ∝ E^-2); two-lens imaging of the source with magnification set by both stacks; absorption limits aperture (transmission falls with N); chromatic focusing gives harmonic rejection up to ~10^5 with slits (PDR); FDR max lens counts: 180 Be for B, 107 Ni for G/2. Zoom trade-off (FDR Fig. 4.4, station B): adding upstream CRL1 lenses enlarges the focal spot (≈0.9 → 8 µm H at 35 keV) but raises transmission (≈0.2 → 0.64 at 35 keV, 0.84 at 15 keV) - the smallest spots cost flux.

interactiveIdeas.title: Old ring vs new ring: how much light is 'in step'?
interactiveIdeas.concept: Side-by-side phase-space ellipses (size × divergence) for the pre-upgrade and upgraded electron beams vs the diffraction-limited ellipse λ/4π at the chosen energy. A counter shows the coherent fraction and coherent flux as the visitor drags the energy from 5 to 100 keV.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: What emittance is, why shrinking it 70× matters most at high energy, and what 'diffraction-limited' means.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Per plane, coherent fraction ≈ (λ/4π)/(Σ·Σ') with Σ = sqrt(σe² + σr²), Σ' = sqrt(σe'² + σr'²), σr = sqrt(2λL)/4π, σr' = sqrt(λ/2L); APS-U flat beam σx 14.5 µm, σx' 2.75 µrad, σy 3.08 µm, σy' 1.29 µrad (r15); old APS σx 280 µm, σx' 11.6 µrad, σy 10 µm, σy' 3.4 µrad (r3); result ≈2% vs 0.01% at 25 keV; energy spread (σδ ≈ 0.14%, r15) further reduces high-harmonic brightness - label as idealised.

interactiveIdeas.title: See-through reactor
interactiveIdeas.concept: A cut-away MOCVD reactor with 2 mm fused-quartz walls; the visitor picks an X-ray energy and sees transmitted total flux and coherent flux curves, finding the sweet spot.
interactiveIdeas.whatUserLearns: Why in situ experiments need high-energy X-rays and why there is an optimum energy for coherent experiments.
interactiveIdeas.physicsToGetRight: Transmission T = exp(-μt) with 4 mm total quartz path (two walls); μ(E) from NIST XCOM/xraylib; multiply by source coherent flux (∝ B·λ²); Ju et al. 2017 (Fig. 2, comparing the then-current 12-ID-D undulator, 3.0 cm × 2.0 m, with projected APS-U sources) give optimum energies of ≈30 keV for total and ≈23 keV for coherent flux transmitted through the 4 mm of quartz (r18).

funFacts: CHEX gets three experiments out of one undulator: two thin diamond crystals each reflect a different harmonic (15 keV, then 25 or 35 keV) and let the rest of the light pass through to the next crystal, and a final silicon crystal picks off 75 or 105 keV (r4, r7, r8, r9).

Two of its fixed-energy beams (D/E and F) are bent sideways by about 23 degrees by diamond crystals - enormous compared with the few-milliradian (a fraction of a degree) deflections of typical synchrotron mirrors, e.g. 4 mrad at 25-ID (r4, r7, r1).
At 75-105 keV, beryllium lenses barely bend X-rays, so CHEX's G station focuses with lenses made of nickel (r1, Table 4.12).

Before the upgrade, scientists had to pull the monochromator out entirely and use a 'pink' beam - the undulator's whole harmonic peak, about 1% wide in energy - just to get enough coherent X-rays to watch GaN grow (r17).
An APS-U-design canted front end was installed at 28-ID and tested with beam on the old ring in November 2018 - a project milestone more than four years before the upgrade dark period began (r3, r2).
In 2017 sector 28 was empty; before CHEX was built it hosted IDEA, a temporary beamline for testing the optics that would preserve the upgraded APS's coherence (r4, r21).
CHEX currently runs on 'stand-in' permanent-magnet undulators; superconducting undulators cooled to 4.2 K are planned to replace them (r10, r13).

Two branches use tandem hutch pairs (B/C and D/E): a beam stop at the end of the front hutch lets teams build and tune a large growth chamber in the back hutch while another experiment runs in front. F and G instead have two positions in one long hutch, where the front instrument moves aside ('beam-pass' mode) to feed the rear one (r1, r4).
The design anticipated about 1 terabyte of data per day from each of the four simultaneous experiments (r4).
The upgraded APS ring's measured emittance (45 pm·rad at 50 mA) beat the previous world record of 134 pm·rad (r16).

CHEX grew out of years of community workshops; a 2018 project listing named Robert Winarski and Brian Stephenson as its science leads, and today's beamline team (Matt Highland, Zhan Zhang, Hua Zhou, Hawoong Hong, Tomoya Kawaguchi) runs it within the APS Surface Scattering and Microdiffraction group (r26, r5, r22).
Superconducting undulators are expected to give about three times the brightness of the interim permanent-magnet undulators above 50 keV (r13).

openQuestions: Which interim undulator feeds which branch is inferred (upstream 2.8 cm → outboard/tunable; downstream 3.0 cm → inboard/fixed) from the APS canting convention (FDR 6-ID and 34-ID text) and FDR power tables; not stated explicitly for 28-ID. The Beamline Directory lists 'SCU0' as the B/C source, which conflicts with the Sep-2026 ID table.
Installation date of the 18.5 mm SCU pair at 28-ID (Strategic Plan: 2026-2027; ID table of 22 Sep 2026 still shows HPMUs). Length conflict: FDR Ch.4 1.3 m vs FDR Ch.3 1.2 m (magnetic).
Tunable-branch energy range conflicts: 5-60 keV (FDR text), 15-60 keV (MEDSI 2025, PDR), 6-30 keV (Directory, Si(111) with interim source), sector-wide 5-104 keV (feature page).
MEDSI 2025 says the selectable-energy branches cover 15-60 keV, but the Directory lists 75/105 keV for G (FDR: 45-105 keV).
Whether the Si(311) DCM crystal pair and the optional double-multilayer monochromator ('DCM or DMM') were installed.
Design and location of the 'twisted monochromator' providing 10 keV for HAXPES in 28-ID-E.

As-built SCM details: diamond thickness, Bragg vs Laue geometry, cooling (FDR says LN2-cooled; PDR emphasised symmetric Bragg), whether D/E also has (022)/(004) crystals, and the exact graphite-filter location.
As-built transfocator models and lens inventories (FDR Table 4.11-4.12 are design values; Ni lenses for G not confirmed as built).
Detector models (PAD type, sensor material, pixel size) and whether the long-distance detector positioners were built as in FDR Fig. 4.8.
Which F position hosts the MOCVD chamber vs the hexapod diffractometer; instrument at G/2.
Whether the C (oxide MBE), E (PLD/HAXPES) and F (MOCVD) systems are the relocated 33-ID-E, 33-ID-D and 12-ID-D instruments (strongly suggested, not stated).

Exact hutch wall positions, widths and heights (values here are scaled from FDR Fig. 4.2 and the 2025 ray-trace plan) and front-end component positions inside the tunnel (only exit mask/collimator are tabulated).
Front-end exit aperture: 2 × 1 mm (CHEX requirement, FDR 4-2.3) vs 2 × 2 mm (standard CUFE, FDR Table 4.6/Ch.3).
Measured flux and focal sizes with the interim HPMUs (FDR Table 4.10 values assume SCUs).
Beamline Directory status fields ('Not Currently Operational' for B/C) appear stale relative to the 5 Oct 2026 commissioning chart (stage 5).
Whether pink/white-beam operation is offered to users in B/C (white-beam stops exist; PDR lists pink beam as an option).
FDR internal inconsistency: Table 4.11 CRL-2 stack sizes for station B sum to 191 two-dimensional 50 µm lenses vs a 180-lens maximum in Table 4.12; the as-built count is unknown.
General-user start date: the Aug 2025 update projected GU entry in run 2026-1 or 2026-2; as of 5 Oct 2026 no CHEX station is at stage 6 and no new date is published.

verification.method: Primary sources re-opened: FDR Ch.1/3/4 text and rendered figures, PDR Ch.6, APS web pages re-fetched on 2026-10-09 (feature page, Beamline Directory 215/237/238/239, ID table, SR parameters, APS news/updates, SSM page, proposal call), the 5 Oct 2026 commissioning chart (rendered), MEDSI'25 TUOA01, arXiv texts of Ju 2017/2019, Lee 2014 full text, Crossref metadata for all journal references; numerical physics (Bragg angles, coherent fractions, speckle criterion, emittance ratios) recomputed.
